title: Power switching: loads, losses and turn-off energy
summary: Put the device into a complete switching path, account for heat and transients, and plan measurements without treating a bench example as machine approval.

blocks.title: The switch is one part of an energy path
blocks.body: A reliable output starts with the source, load, interconnect, switch, protection, driver and thermal path. Choosing a MOSFET by current rating alone skips most of the circuit.

blocks.heading: 1. Classify the load before the switch

columns.name: Resistive
columns.detail: Current largely follows applied voltage. Inrush can still matter when resistance changes with temperature, as with lamps and heaters.

columns.name: Inductive
columns.detail: Coils and motors store magnetic energy. Current resists rapid change, so turn-off requires a defined commutation or clamp path.

columns.name: Capacitive
columns.detail: Charging current can be high at turn-on. Source impedance, precharge and switch safe operating area may control the design.

columns.name: Electromechanical
columns.detail: Solenoids, relays and valves add motion, release-time and fault consequences to their electrical coil behavior.

blocks.heading: 2. Build a loss budget
items: Estimate conduction loss using the appropriate hot on-state parameter: MOSFET I²R or BJT VCE(sat) × I.
Estimate switching loss from voltage-current overlap during transitions. Frequency multiplies energy lost per cycle.
Include gate- or base-drive loss, clamp loss, diode loss, wiring loss and any current-sense element.
Use the manufacturer thermal model and real mounting conditions to estimate junction temperature. Then leave margin and validate with controlled measurements.

blocks.heading: 3. Give inductive current a deliberate path
blocks.body: When an inductive switch opens, current continues in the same direction until stored energy is removed. A freewheel diode can limit voltage but may slow current decay and actuator release. A TVS, Zener-assisted path or active clamp can allow a higher voltage and faster decay, but the switch and clamp must safely absorb the energy. The right answer depends on current, inductance, repetition, timing and equipment behavior.

blocks.title: Do not prototype by modifying a production safety circuit
blocks.body: This course explains components. It does not approve bypassing guards, changing emergency-stop circuits or attaching unreviewed hardware to a controller output. Use isolated supplies where required, follow lockout procedures and have machine changes reviewed under the applicable electrical and safety standards.

blocks.heading: 4. Plan a controlled bring-up
items: Review schematic, polarity, grounding and component ratings with power removed.
Set a current-limited supply conservatively and start with a representative safe load or fixture, not the machine actuator.
Measure gate or base drive relative to the local device reference. Measure switch voltage and load current with probes and instruments rated for the circuit.
Capture turn-on, steady state and turn-off. Check overshoot, ringing, release time and temperature under worst intended conditions.
Record the setup and limits. A successful short test is evidence for that setup, not automatic production qualification.

blocks.heading: 5. Check the model
blocks.prompt: A plain flyback diode keeps a solenoid switch voltage low. What tradeoff may appear?
options: The coil current can decay more slowly, delaying release.
The controller supplies no gate current.
blocks.explanation: A low clamp voltage removes magnetic energy slowly. A higher clamp can speed release, but it raises switch and clamp stress and must be designed accordingly.

items.label: Define normal and fault cases
items.detail: Include open load, short circuit, reversed supply, stalled motion and repeated switching where relevant.

items.label: Trace stored energy
items.detail: For each inductive or capacitive element, state where its energy goes at switching events.

items.label: Close the thermal loop
items.detail: Connect losses to package, interface, heat sink or board, ambient and maximum junction temperature.

items.label: Define acceptance evidence
items.detail: Name the waveforms, temperatures, timing and fault responses that must be measured before release.
